passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 11, Friday.
Dolma has come to Thursday sessions for two months. Her parents support it, but have asked her to tell relatives she is at "extra maths", because an aunt keeps worrying aloud about what people will say, with her elder sister's marriage talks going on. Dolma says the lie itself is exhausting. At lunch she sits alone so no one asks where she goes on Thursdays, and she says she feels as if she's living behind glass.
Today we made a list of people she might trust. She chose one: her lab partner Abhinav, who once mentioned his own brother's counselling. What I did next: we practised what she might say, and she agreed I could check in. She came back after lunch looking lighter. "He just said thanks for telling him, and asked if I want company on Thursdays," she said. She smiled for most of the session.

qa.q: What have Dolma's parents asked her to tell relatives?
qa.a: That she is at "extra maths".

qa.q: How does Dolma feel about keeping the secret?
qa.a: Lonely and exhausted, as if living behind glass.

qa.q: What step did the counsellor help Dolma take?
qa.a: Choosing one trusted person, Abhinav, and practising what to say before telling him.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Dolma's news, given his own brother's counselling?
qa.a: He likely sees it as ordinary and nothing to be ashamed of, which is why he thanked her and offered company on Thursdays.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose family hides her counselling out of fear of gossip and marriage worries, whose secrecy brings loneliness, and who feels relief telling a trusted person.

passage:
Sunday, after Pinky Didi's wedding.
Everyone kept asking why I'd missed so much school this term. Mummy answered for me every time: "Typhoid, poor thing." It wasn't typhoid. The doctor gave what I have a name months ago, and I see a psychologist every week. But Mummy says if anyone finds out, the whole family will talk, and Didi's in-laws might think something runs in our family. So I smiled and lied all day, and felt like the loneliest person in a hall of four hundred people.
Then my cousin Chaitanya found me on the back steps. He said, "You don't have to tell me anything. You just look tired." I told him. Not the name, just that I'm getting help. He said, "Okay. I'm glad you are." That's all. No fuss.
For the first time all day, my chest unknotted. Maybe I get to choose who knows.
Kamal

qa.q: What did Mummy tell people every time?
qa.a: Typhoid, poor thing.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel at the wedding, and why?
qa.a: Kamal felt like the loneliest person in a hall of four hundred people, because of smiling and lying all day to hide the truth.

qa.q: What choice on the back steps changed Kamal's day?
qa.a: Kamal chose to tell one trusted person, Chaitanya, only as much as felt right, and felt relief.

qa.q: Why might Mummy feel the need to hide it?
qa.a: She fears the family's gossip and that Didi's in-laws might judge, so hiding feels like protection to her.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose family conceals a diagnosis to avoid gossip and marriage worries, and how secrecy brings loneliness while choosing a trusted cousin brings relief.

passage: Reena, you asked why I always said I had tuition on Thursdays. I'm Wasim, and the truth is I was going to a counsellor. Ammi made me promise not to tell anyone, not even Nani. She kept saying, "Log kya kahenge? Your sister's rishta is being discussed. If people hear you see a doctor for your mind..." So I lied to everyone. To you, to the cricket boys. It was like carrying a stone inside my shirt all the time. I felt so alone. The counsellor helped, but the hiding was making me worse. Last month I decided to tell just you, because I trust you. You didn't gossip. You just said, "Okay. Want to come to tuition-that-isn't-tuition together?" I laughed so hard. I felt lighter immediately.

qa.q: What did Wasim tell people he had on Thursdays?
qa.a: Tuition.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel while hiding the counselling?
qa.a: Wasim felt lonely and weighed down, like carrying a stone inside a shirt.

qa.q: What helped ease Wasim's loneliness?
qa.a: Choosing one trusted friend, Reena, to tell, who responded with kindness and humour instead of gossip.

qa.q: How might Wasim's Ammi see the counselling?
qa.a: She seems frightened of gossip and her daughter's marriage prospects, so she wants it kept secret.

grounding: Shows a teenager hiding counselling because of fear of gossip and marriage worries, lonely in the secrecy, and relieved after telling a trusted friend.

passage:
Monday: After the psychologist said Minakshi, fifteen, had depression, her mother drove home in silence. At the gate she said, "Don't tell anyone. Not your friends, not your aunts. Your didi's wedding talks are going on."
Thursday: At school Minakshi said she'd been "sick with fever" when asked where she'd been. At lunch she sat apart, feeling like everyone could see through her. She had never felt so alone.
The next Monday: On the walk home, her friend Raghav said, "You've been so far away. Are you okay?" She took a breath and told him, just him. He was quiet, then said, "My brother sees a counsellor too. I'm glad you told me." For the first time in a week, Minakshi's chest loosened.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say she had been sick with?
qa.a: Fever.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel at school on Thursday?
qa.a: She felt lonely and anxious, as if everyone could see through her lie.

qa.q: What choice brought Minakshi relief?
qa.a: She chose to tell one trusted friend, Raghav, who responded with understanding instead of judgment.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Minakshi told him?
qa.a: Raghav may have felt trusted and glad she opened up, even sharing about his brother.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose family hides her diagnosis for fear of gossip and a sister's wedding, lonely in secrecy, and relieved after telling a trusted friend.

passage: "Sahil, you're telling everyone you have football practice on Saturday, when really you're seeing a counsellor? I know, beta. Your Pema Bua did the same. When I was sixteen, in Kalimpong, I saw a counsellor after my father died. My mother said, 'Don't tell anyone. People will say the girl is mad, who will marry her?' So I hid it. I lied to my best friend. I ate lunch alone so no one would ask. The secret was heavier than the sadness. Then one day I told Tsering, my closest friend, only her. She hugged me and said, 'I'm glad you're getting help.' That day I felt I could breathe. You don't have to tell everyone. But choose one person you trust."

qa.q: Where did Pema Bua live when she was sixteen?
qa.a: In Kalimpong.

qa.q: How did young Pema feel while hiding her counselling?
qa.a: She felt lonely and weighed down, finding the secret heavier than the sadness.

qa.q: What turning point in the story brought young Pema relief?
qa.a: Telling one trusted friend, Tsering, who hugged her and said she was glad Pema was getting help.

qa.q: How did Pema's mother see the counselling back then?
qa.a: She feared gossip and marriage prospects, seeing it as something to hide.

grounding: An elder recalls hiding counselling due to fear of gossip and marriage worries, feeling lonely, and finding relief in telling one trusted friend.

passage:
The house in Ludhiana was full of aunties for Jasleen's sister's engagement, and everyone was talking about the boy's family. So when the school counsellor's reminder buzzed on her phone for Thursday, Jasleen quickly hid it.
Mummy had said it clearly: "No one outside this house knows about the counselling. Log kya kahenge? Your sister's rishta could break."
So Jasleen smiled at every aunty and said she was "fine, just exams." Inside she felt more alone than ever. At night she lay awake, anxious someone would find out.
Her cousin Deepak found her on the terrace while the others were dancing. "You look like you're somewhere else."
She hesitated. Deepak had always kept her secrets. "I see a counsellor. For my anxiety. Nobody can know."
Deepak just sat down beside her. "That's good. I'm glad you have someone." Jasleen felt her shoulders loosen. For the first time in weeks, she wasn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: Where did Deepak find Jasleen?
qa.a: On the terrace, while the others were dancing.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel while hiding the counselling from the aunties?
qa.a: She felt lonely and anxious, lying awake at night worried someone would find out.

qa.q: What choice brought Jasleen relief, and why?
qa.a: Choosing to tell a trusted person, Deepak, who had always kept her secrets; sharing eased the loneliness that the secrecy caused.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the counselling differently if gossip weren't a worry?
qa.a: She might feel free to support Jasleen openly and proud she's getting help, instead of fearing for the rishta.

grounding: Jasleen hides her counselling from relatives to avoid gossip and marriage worries, feels lonely, and finds relief by telling a trusted cousin.
